Build a complete, production-ready cross-platform interface design system and reference implementation that uses an original dynamic translucent material named **Prismatic Surface**. Do not mention, reproduce, or depend on any pre-existing software product, operating system, framework-specific proprietary visual system, trademark, source code, assets, or brand identity.

Construct the entire project from scratch and provide every required file in full, unabridged form: repository structure, package manifests, build configuration, source code, type definitions, styling, tests, documentation, accessibility configuration, linting, formatting, continuous-integration configuration, and deployment instructions. Do not use placeholders, mock implementations, dummy data, omitted sections, pseudocode, ellipses, or incomplete snippets. The result must build, run, test, and deploy as delivered.

Create a unified visual language for responsive web, tablet, desktop, television, and wearable-sized interfaces. The system must preserve platform-appropriate layout density and input behavior while sharing a consistent material, motion model, typography scale, color-token model, icon treatment, navigation model, and component behavior across every target form factor.

Implement **Prismatic Surface** as a dynamic translucent interface material with all of the following characteristics:

- It must visually resemble physically plausible glass without copying any named third-party design language.
- It must transmit the visual influence of content behind it through configurable transparency, backdrop blur, saturation adjustment, tinting, contrast correction, and edge treatment.
- It must simulate reflected and refracted surrounding color through layered gradients, directional light, clipping, blur, and compositing.
- It must adapt its tint, luminance, opacity, border contrast, shadow, and text/icon foreground colors based on the estimated brightness and dominant color characteristics of the content behind it.
- It must support both light and dark themes and smoothly transition between themes without flashing, unreadable intermediate states, or unstable contrast.
- It must support real-time movement response through pointer position, device orientation where permission is available, scroll position, focus state, active state, hover state, and component transition state.
- It must render controlled specular highlights that move across the material surface according to the active input signal, remain visually subtle, and never reduce the readability of labels or controls.
- It must have a deterministic static fallback when real-time rendering, backdrop filtering, motion sensors, or high-performance graphics features are unavailable.
- It must respect user preferences for reduced motion, reduced transparency, increased contrast, forced colors, color-scheme preference, and battery-saving or low-performance environments.

Use a layered rendering architecture. Define a background-content layer, an adaptive backdrop-sampling layer, a refraction-and-blur layer, a tint-and-color-correction layer, a specular-highlight layer, a border-and-inner-glow layer, a foreground-content layer, and an accessibility fallback layer. Ensure that each layer is independently configurable through design tokens and that the final compositing order is documented and tested.

Implement the material with progressive enhancement. Use standards-based CSS custom properties, `backdrop-filter`, `filter`, `color-mix`, gradients, masks where supported, and GPU-friendly transforms. Add feature detection for unsupported browser capabilities. Provide a robust opaque or semi-opaque fallback that preserves hierarchy, interaction affordances, and text contrast without relying on backdrop blur, transparency, motion effects, or experimental APIs.

Create a complete token system with semantic and component-level tokens. Include tokens for light and dark modes; surface opacity; blur strength; saturation; luminance lift; adaptive tint; border alpha; inner highlight alpha; outer shadow; corner radius; elevation; focus ring; content foreground colors; disabled states; hover states; pressed states; selected states; destructive actions; success states; warning states; and informational states. Include tokens for compact, regular, and spacious density modes. Define all tokens in a machine-readable source format and generate typed runtime exports and CSS variables from that source.

Build all major components using Prismatic Surface where appropriate:

- Buttons: primary, secondary, tertiary, destructive, icon-only, split-button, loading, disabled, and toggle variants.
- Form controls: text inputs, password inputs, search inputs, text areas, selects, comboboxes, checkboxes, radios, switches, sliders, segmented controls, date/time inputs, file uploads, validation states, and error messages.
- Navigation: top bar, bottom bar, sidebar, tabs, breadcrumbs, pagination, command palette, contextual menus, dropdown menus, overflow menus, and keyboard navigation.
- Containers: cards, panels, sheets, drawers, dialogs, popovers, tooltips, toasts, banners, accordions, disclosure groups, and inspector panels.
- Data presentation: tables, sortable columns, responsive table layouts, lists, tree views, badges, avatars, empty states, progress indicators, charts with accessible text equivalents, media controls, and status indicators.
- Application-shell elements: home/dashboard grid, lock-screen-style notification view, control-center-style quick settings surface, desktop dock, launcher grid, window chrome, toolbar, and command area.
- Widget system: small, medium, and large responsive widgets that can present live status, media, calendar, weather-like data structures, controls, and summary content without relying on proprietary service APIs.

Use the dynamic material selectively. Apply it to high-level navigation chrome, floating controls, toolbars, panels, sheets, dialogs, sidebars, tabs, media controls, widgets, quick settings, dock-like navigation, and relevant interactive elements. Avoid excessive layering: prevent nested translucent surfaces from producing muddy contrast or excessive GPU compositing. Define strict compositing budgets and enforce them through tests or runtime warnings.

Implement responsive behavior for at least five layout ranges: wearable, phone, tablet, desktop, and television. For each range, define breakpoints, typography, touch-target requirements, keyboard behavior, focus behavior, content density, navigation transformations, panel behavior, modal behavior, and safe-area handling. Support mouse, keyboard, touch, stylus, gamepad-style directional input where available, and assistive technologies.

Implement a performance architecture that targets smooth interaction on modern hardware and graceful degradation on constrained hardware. Avoid continuous JavaScript animation loops when CSS or compositor-driven animations can be used. Throttle or pause motion calculations when the document is hidden, when reduced motion is enabled, when the user is not interacting, or when performance heuristics indicate repeated dropped frames. Use `requestAnimationFrame` only for active visual updates that cannot be represented declaratively. Clean up all event listeners, observers, animation frames, and sensor subscriptions.

Implement adaptive backdrop analysis without collecting or transmitting user data. The system may analyze local rendered colors or explicitly supplied background metadata to choose readable surface and foreground tokens, but it must not capture screenshots, upload pixels, fingerprint devices, or make network requests for visual analysis. Provide an API that allows application code to supply background luminance and dominant-color hints when automatic estimation is not possible.

Meet accessibility requirements throughout the implementation:

- Ensure all text and essential icons meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast requirements in every supported theme and fallback mode.
- Ensure controls retain visible boundaries and understandable states when transparency is reduced or disabled.
- Support keyboard-only navigation, visible focus indicators, logical focus order, focus trapping in modal components, Escape handling where applicable, and restoration of focus after dialogs close.
- Use semantic HTML first, ARIA only where needed, and correct ARIA roles, states, labels, live regions, and descriptions.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-reduced-transparency` where supported, `prefers-contrast`, `forced-colors`, and system dark-mode settings.
- Ensure motion effects do not convey essential information alone.
- Provide screen-reader text and nonvisual alternatives for charts, indicators, icons, and custom controls.
- Test every component with automated accessibility checks and document manual keyboard and screen-reader verification procedures.

Create a demonstrator application that uses the complete component library rather than isolated component samples. Include a dashboard, navigation shell, media view, settings view, profile view, notification view, command palette, modal workflows, data table workflow, form validation workflow, theme controls, contrast controls, reduced-transparency controls, and reduced-motion controls. Populate the demonstrator only with internally defined, meaningful application content and deterministic local data. Do not depend on remote APIs, external credentials, third-party analytics, or proprietary content.

Implement theme and preference controls that immediately update the entire interface. Include system-default, forced-light, forced-dark, high-contrast, reduced-transparency, and reduced-motion modes. Persist user choices locally with explicit versioned storage and a migration strategy. Provide a reset-to-system-default control. Ensure preference changes never cause inaccessible text, flashing, focus loss, layout jumps, or temporary unstyled content.

Provide full automated testing:

- Unit tests for token generation, color calculations, luminance estimation, contrast calculations, fallback selection, theme persistence, and interaction-state transitions.
- Component tests for all component variants, keyboard interactions, focus management, validation states, disabled states, error states, and responsive rendering.
- Visual regression tests for light mode, dark mode, high contrast, reduced transparency, reduced motion, and all responsive layout ranges.
- End-to-end tests for navigation, settings persistence, dialogs, command palette, tables, forms, theme transitions, and accessibility preference changes.
- Accessibility tests using an automated accessibility engine and documented manual validation scripts.
- Performance tests that measure render cost, input latency, animation frame stability, and surface-layer counts.
- Cross-browser tests for current stable Chromium-based browsers, Firefox, and WebKit-based browsers.

Include complete developer documentation. Document installation, local development, build commands, test commands, architecture, rendering layers, token schema, theming, accessibility behavior, responsive strategy, performance budgets, browser support, fallback behavior, component APIs, contribution workflow, release process, and deployment process. Document every public API with type signatures and usage examples that correspond exactly to the delivered implementation.

Set explicit quality gates. The project must fail continuous integration if type checking fails, linting fails, formatting checks fail, unit tests fail, visual-regression tests fail, accessibility tests reveal serious or critical violations, production builds fail, generated token outputs differ from their sources, or performance budgets are exceeded. Configure dependency locking, reproducible builds, environment validation, security auditing, and license reporting.

Do not use copied visual assets, proprietary assets, third-party marks, external image hotlinking, or an existing product’s interface structure. Create all visual assets, icons, illustrations, gradients, typography decisions, and example content independently within the repository. Ensure the system is a standalone original implementation whose appearance is defined by translucent adaptive surfaces, real-time visual response, strong legibility, and accessible fallback behavior.
